en: A coastal site eroding into the sea just south of Kissonerga, dug by Edgar Peltenburg's Lemba Archaeological Project between 1976 and 1996. Its earliest phase survives as almost nothing but wells: cylindrical shafts eight and seven metres deep, cut into bedrock with hand and footholds, among the oldest water wells known anywhere in the world. Nothing comparable is found on the Levantine mainland until much later, which suggests the settlers had to invent their own answer to a dry island. The wells were later filled with rubbish, animal carcasses and human bone, and that rubbish is now the richest single source we have for the first farmers of Cyprus.

A cylindrical shaft at least 8 m deep cut into unweathered bedrock, with hand and footholds carved down the sides for climbing in and out. It is the only trace of the site's earliest occupation, and one of the two or three oldest water wells known from anywhere on earth. Specialists prefer 'among the earliest known' to 'the world's oldest', because the Cypriot wells and those at Shillourokambos overlap in date.
